result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A separates what's fine from what isn't, puts phone-only cancellation first as the core problem, and gives replacement wording for every screen without citing any laws or statistics. B covers the same problems well, but it brings in specific legal claims (California ARL, EU dates, the FTC rule being vacated), which breaks item 5. Its problem list also isn't ordered by severity, and its 'Sorry to see you go' rewrite barely changes anything. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B handles the stat claim better: it says to drop it unless sourced and gives a neutral replacement template. It also puts phone-only cancellation first as the worst problem and rewrites every screen. A catches the same core problems but lists them out of severity order. It also adds statute and regulation citations (California ARL, the EU 2026 date, the FTC rule being vacated), which the rubric penalises, and some of these are shaky. B's approval of the pause offer, the optional reason question and a single equal-weight save screen also matches item 1 more closely than A's blanket 'yes, dark pattern'.
